Christie's International Real Estate enters mainland China with Shanghai agency
article:
Luxury real estate brokerage firm Christie's International Real Estate has expanded into mainland China for the first time with the launch of an affiliate in Shanghai.

The new agency, Christie's International Real Estate Shanghai, is led by managing director Stephenie Zhou, a real estate adviser with experience spanning new development sales and marketing, as well as the resale of historic homes in Shanghai.

The Shanghai affiliate will focus on the city’s prime residential submarkets, including Xintiandi and The Bund.

Over the past decade, Zhou and her team have handled transactions involving historic homes, luxury apartments and villas in these areas, with prices ranging from RMB28 million to RMB300 million ($5.1 million to $57.2 million).

The team will combine its local market expertise and developer relationships with Christie’s International Real Estate's global network, marketing programmes and referral capabilities.

It will also target international advisory and referral opportunities amid growing interest among high-net-worth Chinese buyers in overseas properties, driven by family, education and business ties.

The expansion comes as China’s residential property market continues to adjust following several challenging years. Fitch Ratings expects nationwide new home sales to fall 11% to 13% y-o-y in 2026, although tier-one cities have continued to outperform lower-tier markets, with demand in stronger cities skewed towards larger and higher-priced projects.

According to Zhou, Shanghai’s luxury residential segment has shown greater resilience. She has observed steady price growth among luxury new developments since the beginning of 2026, alongside signs of stabilisation in the resale market and improving buyer confidence.

Branded residences are also becoming a more significant part of Shanghai's luxury residential market, amid demand for homes offering higher-end design, amenities, services and lifestyle experiences.

The Shanghai launch extends Christie's International Real Estate's expansion across Asia Pacific (Apac). Over the past two years, the network has established new affiliates in Hong Kong, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, Australia and New Zealand.

Helena Moyas de Forton, managing director for Europe, the Middle East and Africa as well as Apac at Christie's International Real Estate, said Shanghai is an important market for the network given the increasingly international interests and investments of its luxury clientele.

The company has close ties to the separately owned Christie's auction house. In 2024, the auction house opened its 50,000 sq ft Apac headquarters at The Henderson in Hong Kong, which hosts auctions, exhibitions and private client events.

title: Singapore court appoints KPMG to manage trader Radiant World
article:
(Sept 24): A Singapore court appointed KPMG restructuring executives to take control of Radiant World on Thursday, granting an application by creditor Mizuho Bank Ltd, which has accused the trader of an alleged fraud linked to iron ore receivables.

The KPMG executives Toh Ai Ling, Adrian Chan and Tan Yen Chiaw will be interim judicial managers of Radiant World Corporation Pte, the trader’s key operating entity in the country, according to people familiar with the decision, speaking after a court conference.

Under judicial management, an independent manager is appointed by the court to take control of a company in financial distress, with the aim of rehabilitating it or allowing the creditors to reach a compromise. Interim judicial management is a step typically taken by creditors as they seek to preserve assets.

KPMG, Mizuho and Radiant World did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Mizuho’s lawyers at Shook Lin & Bok declined to comment.

Thursday’s decision marks a significant escalation in the crisis surrounding Radiant World, once a major participant in the iron ore trade. Mizuho is suing the trader over US$97.3 million ($124.4 million) in receivables purportedly arising from iron ore sales to Glencore International AG, according to a court filing obtained by Bloomberg News.

The bank later said it had strong reasons to believe it had been the victim of fraud.

See also: Arnault tightens grip on LVMH with simpler holding structure

title: Arnault tightens grip on LVMH with simpler holding structure
article:
(Sept 24): Bernard Arnault and his family plan to simplify the ownership structure of LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE to ensure control of the world’s biggest luxury group is preserved across generations.

As a result of the plan, almost all of the Arnault family’s stake in the group would be held in a single listed entity, Agache SCA, replacing the major LVMH holding company Christian Dior SE.

It’s the latest in a series of moves by Arnault, 77, to tighten the family’s control over the company he built and prepare it for an eventual succession as investors increasingly seek clarity on the issue.

LVMH shares were little changed in Paris on Thursday. They have slumped almost 40% this year, amid trouble at its most profitable brand Louis Vuitton in China.

Agache, a limited joint-stock partnership, would hold a direct stake in LVMH of 49.76% of the share capital and 65.55% of the voting rights after the latest changes are completed. Known in France as a société en commandite par actions, the structure is used by families to cement their grip over a group — legal experts call it a “padlock.”

Ever since the 1980s, when he acquired fashion house Christian Dior and founded LVMH, Arnault has maneuvered to consolidate his control. One of his biggest transactions came in 2017 when he offered to buy out minority shareholders in Christian Dior for €12 billion (US$13.7 billion or $17.5 billion).

See also: Uber to cut 3,300 jobs in overhaul to reduce management layers

In the latest plan, a multi-step process would see the family’s holdings merged into Christian Dior, before it is renamed Agache SCA. That would make Agache the family’s main holding company, replacing Christian Dior as its listed vehicle.

“Upon completion of these transactions, control over LVMH would thus be exercised within a single company, listed on Euronext Paris for over thirty years,” Christian Dior said in a statement Wednesday.

See also: Western Union probed in Australia over laundering controls

The effort to keep the limited joint-stock partnership listed was questioned by some, given the minuscule portion that’s likely to be held by outside investors.

“The logic would be not to list Agache SCA at all,” said Pascal Quiry, corporate finance professor at business school HEC Paris. That’s because “so little is likely to be floating after the offer, at most 1%, and since LVMH is already controlled by the Arnault family anyway,” he said.

As part of the replacement of Christian Dior, minority shareholders will have the option to sell their shares in a tender offer, or remain shareholders alongside the Arnault family within LVMH’s yet-to-be created controlling entity Agache.

Shares of Christian Dior rose as much as 19% on Thursday.

The Arnault family would be required under stock market rules to make a tender offer, to be paid in cash, for all the Dior shares it doesn’t own, representing 2.44% of the share capital. As of Tuesday, the value of that stake is around €1.63 billion, according to the statement.

An extraordinary general meeting of Christian Dior shareholders to approve the changes would likely take place before the end of this year, with the tender offer scheduled for the first quarter of next year subject to clearance from the regulator AMF. The tender offer would not be followed by a squeeze-out.

title: Trump and Xi buy time on trade with neither able to afford a fight
article:
(Sept 24): US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping agreed to maintain a trade truce until early 2027, with neither ready to upend relations between the world’s biggest economies even as tensions persist over rare earths, technology curbs and Taiwan.

Just as Xi landed in the US on Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that an agreement struck by the leaders last year will now run an additional two months until Jan 10. That removes much of the tension around Xi’s first state visit to the US since 2015, and clears the way for two more meetings between the presidents planned in the coming months at summits in Shenzhen and Miami.

Still, the brief extension shows that the “constructive strategic stability” underpinning the relationship remains fragile. The US has accused China of failing to live up to pledges to provide a steady flow of rare earths, while Beijing remains confident that its grip over the elements crucial to defense and high-tech manufacturing will deter Trump from reimposing sky-high tariffs.

“We can live with that because we are confident that within two months the US cannot become independent of Chinese rare-earth supply,” said Wu Xinbo, a director of Fudan University’s Center for American Studies and a former adviser to China’s Foreign Ministry. “They’ll come back and beg for Chinese exports of rare earth magnets to the US.”

News of the extension appeared to reduce the immediate risk of a supply disruption, hurting shares of companies seeking to provide alternatives to Chinese rare earth supplies. Toyo Engineering Corp slid about 9% in Tokyo and Australia’s Lynas Rare Earths Ltd fell as much as 5%. The broader markets showed little enthusiasm, with China’s benchmark CSI 300 Index falling 1.7% and MSCI’s gauge of Asian stocks dropping 0.8%, also pressured by elevated oil prices and US bond yields.

See also: US unveils two-month truce extension as Xi lands for summit

Bessent on Wednesday met with his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng in Washington to hammer out the terms, building from talks held in New York last weekend. Even so, the US Treasury secretary made his displeasure clear while announcing the truce.

“There are some deliverables that have not been perfect on the Chinese side,” Bessent told Fox News. US officials had spelled out their expectations and now wanted to see if Beijing “could be a bit more fulsome in enacting the agreement” in the coming months.

Both sides appear to have settled for less than expected. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer indicated this week the US was looking to extend the truce for three to six months while highlighting the lack of trust between the nations. China had sought a longer period, aiming to lock in the current deal through the Trump presidency.

See also: China’s selective crop buying tests US trade truce before summit

Agriculture is another source of dissatisfaction on the US side. China is about than halfway toward meeting its pledge to buy 25 million tons of US soybeans this year, but progress has been slower on a separate commitment to purchase about US$17 billion ($21.76 billion) in additional American agricultural goods.

“We are encouraging them to pick those up,” Bessent said on Wednesday.

The lack of tangible progress on trade didn’t stop Trump from rolling out the red carpet for Xi at Joint Base Andrews, where he became the first US president in six decades to receive a foreign counterpart, excluding visits by the Pope. The two will hold more substantive meetings and a state dinner on Thursday in Washington.

“The summit is producing managed stabilisation,” said Han Lin, the China country director of The Asia Group, adding that the truce extension fulfilled the low expectations held by both sides entering the gathering. “If Trump and Xi do meet again in November or December, maybe the goal is to save the best for last.”

China has sought to keep US tariffs at a relatively low level while also pushing Trump to eliminate national-security restrictions and hold off on any weapons sales to Taiwan. Although the two sides have sought to boost trade in non-sensitive items, they’ve made little progress on a Board of Investment that could open the door for Chinese companies to expand operations in the US — a prospect that faces widespread opposition in the US Congress.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

China is also seeing trade tensions rise with Europe, where leaders have grown increasingly concerned about the erosion of manufacturing in the face of Chinese exports of electric vehicles, consumer electronics and other cutting-edge goods.

“Potential tariff risks from the US and European Union represent potential downside risks to China’s export outlook,” said Lynn Song, the chief economist for Greater China at ING Bank NV in Hong Kong. “It becomes increasingly important for China to shore up domestic demand moving forward.”

Both leaders are also facing domestic challenges that would become more difficult with a wider trade fight. Trump, 80, is approaching November’s midterm elections with his fellow Republicans at risk of losses that could weaken his position in Congress. Xi, 73, is contending with sluggish economic growth, weak domestic demand and elevated youth unemployment ahead of a year that will see the Communist Party pick new leaders at a twice-a-decade gathering.

“Looking at the broader bilateral relationship, neither side can afford more turmoil at this point,” said Zhao Hai, the vice-president of the Chinese Institute of Hong Kong, a think tank affiliated with the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, a government research group in Beijing. “Especially a further escalation that would result in a lose-lose situation.”

title: CSE Global secures two major electrification contracts in US worth $190.5 mil
article:
CSE Global (SGX:544 ) announced that it has secured two major contracts worth US$150.0 million ($190.5 million) in the US.

The first contract involves in the design and manufacture of power distribution centres (PDCs), together with the integration of complex electrical and control systems and equipment in the US for the Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) market.

“The contract is scheduled for execution between 2026 and 2028 and support the expansion of the Calcasieu Pass 2 (CP2) LNG project in Louisiana, which will add LNG processing and associated infrastructure to increase the facility’s production and export capacity,” CSE Global explains.

For the second contract, it is a follow-on order for the design and manufacture of PDCs for the Cheyenne Power Hub project in the US, which was announced on Aug 14. CSE Global adds that these PDCs will form a critical part of the power infrastructure, enabling the safe and reliable distribution of power to the adjacent data centre.

The contract is expected to be executed progressively between 2026 and 2027.

“Rising demand for electrification solutions in the USA’s LNG and power infrastructure markets presents significant opportunities for the Group and will support our continued growth in the Electrification business segment,” says Lim Boon Kheng, group managing director and CEO of CSE Global.

See also: Seatrium completes seventh LNGC to FSRU conversion for Karpowership

CSE Global expects both contracts to have no material impact on its consolidated net tangible assets per share or earnings per share for the current financial year.

Shares of CSE Global closed 2 cents higher, or up 1.61% at $1.26 on Sept 24.

title: Cybersecurity stocks are so hot, investors question staying power
article:
(Sept 24): The shares of cybersecurity companies have soared in recent months on bets that the threats posed by cutting-edge AI models will be a boon for their businesses. But some of the stocks have run up so much that investors are questioning whether they’ve gone too far.

A basket of cybersecurity stocks tracked by Goldman Sachs has more than doubled since hitting a low on April 10 after Anthropic restricted the release of its Mythos AI model over concerns it could power cyberattacks. Crowdstrike Holdings Inc, Palo Alto Networks Inc and Fortinet Inc have all gained more than 130% since then, putting them among the 10 best performers in the S&P 500 over that span.

The rapid gains have made the stocks some of the most expensive in the market. CrowdStrike is priced at more than 170 times estimated earnings, which is second only to Tesla Inc in the S&P 500, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Palo Alto Networks is the fifth-most expensive in the index at 91 times profit projected over the next 12 months. Fortinet’s multiple of 48 ranks 16th.

“If you’re looking to get in now, you have to recognise that what you’re paying reflects the expectation that everything will be perfect in the future,” said Brad Long, chief investment officer at Wealthspire, which has about US$593 billion in assets. “The tailwinds for cybersecurity are obvious, but if we see any weakness — if the AI capex cycle slows, or even if we stop seeing so many sophisticated AI attacks — then their revenue could slow and the stocks could sell off materially.”

The rally is in stark contrast to the beginning of the year, when AI disruption fears sparked an indiscriminate selloff across the software industry. While those worries have subsided for many software companies amid strong financial performance in the sector, a series of recent warnings from within the AI industry about grave threats posed by the technology have provided investors with another reason to buy cybersecurity stocks.

See also: BlackRock, IFM closing in on US$25 bil Asia data centre deal — Bloomberg

The Goldman cybersecurity basket has jumped 19% since Sept 11, the last trading day before Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei called for slowing development of the most advanced models.

With the need for stronger cybersecurity defences now widely accepted, the question is whether the companies can deliver revenue and profit growth to satisfy expectations implied by their nose-bleed valuations.

See also: EV sales are booming in Europe with gasoline at US$10 a gallon

“Cybersecurity may have gotten over its skis,” Bernstein analyst Peter Weed recently cautioned while cutting his ratings on Palo Alto, Okta Inc and SentinelOne Inc.

While the group is seeing real demand, “implicit in the sector stock prices seem to be a degree of acceleration that could rival consumption software like hyperscaler compute or databases,” he wrote in a Sept 17 note. But cybersecurity growth is likely to be constrained by practical factors like customers’ employee headcount, Weed said.

Still, fundamentals appear to be heading in the right direction. In late August, a better-than-expected revenue forecast from CrowdStrike sent the stock up more than 20% the day after earnings, the most since 2019.

“The Mythos moment translated into mass-market acceptance that AI adoption needs security,” chief executive officer George Kurtz said in a statement in the earnings report. “Every enterprise will run on AI, and securing it is the largest market opportunity in our history.”

There have been a number of AI-assisted hacks this year, as well as breaches by AI agents that have alarmed cybersecurity experts and AI developers.

On Thursday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI model had hacked a government website earlier this year, gaining unauthorised access to files on a site for reporting healthcare statistics.

In July, OpenAI said its AI models inadvertently hacked Hugging Face Inc. Last week, Google revealed its Gemini AI model made similar incursions into three company systems during security testing.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

“We believe the market is increasingly pricing in a step-function increase in cyber risk, supporting both higher security spending and a more constructive valuation framework across the sector,” Bank of America analyst Tal Liani wrote in a Sept 18 note. He called cybersecurity “a mega-theme and enabler of the AI era” while raising his price targets on CrowdStrike, Okta, and SailPoint Inc.

Despite the run-up in cybersecurity stock prices, valuation signals can be deceiving if growth outpaces expectations, according to Josh Taves, managing director at Post Oak Group.

“I understand if people are approaching security with a little more trepidation given how much it has risen this year, but while I expect budgets for other kinds of software will decrease as AI models take over, security spending should hold strong or even increase,” he said. “Traditional valuation metrics don’t hold as much water in an environment like this. Investors will pay more because the demand backdrop is so strong.”

Meta Platforms Inc unveiled a palm-sized, dedicated gadget for using Muse, the company’s popular new artificial intelligence assistant, pushing deeper into the AI devices market with a surprise announcement.

Meta also launched US$1,299 virtual-reality glasses that undercut Apple Inc in price and size while putting its headset line on track for profitability.

The company is expanding its smart-glasses lineup with camera-free models, support for the popular new Muse assistant and a hearing-aid mode.

title: BlackRock, IFM closing in on US$25 bil Asia data centre deal — Bloomberg
article:
(Sept 24): A consortium backed by BlackRock Inc and IFM Investors Pty has entered exclusive talks for a potential acquisition of Stack Infrastructure Inc’s Asia-Pacific data centres, people familiar with the matter said.

The investor group — which includes the BlackRock-backed Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure Partnership, known as AIP, as well as IFM — is preparing to conduct due diligence on the assets, the people said. A deal could value the portfolio at around US$20 billion to US$25 billion ($25.6 billion to $32 billion), according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the information is private.

The suitors aim to reach an agreement soon with Stack’s owner, Blue Owl Capital Inc, the people said. Bloomberg News reported previously that Stack was considering a sale of the data centres and that AIP and IFM were among potential bidders. Blue Owl was initially seeking a valuation of more than US$30 billion for the assets, people with knowledge of the matter said previously.

Deliberations are ongoing and talks could drag on or fall apart, the people said. Other suitors may also still be interested in the assets, they added.

Data centres and related infrastructure have come to the forefront of dealmaking in Asia, with global funds seeking exposure to a sector and region riding high on AI’s rapid growth. Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump are meeting this week to discuss issues including AI, with neither showing any intention of slowing down development despite warnings of potential dangers.

AIP’s founders include BlackRock’s Global Infrastructure Partners, Microsoft Corp and Mubadala Investment Co-backed MGX. The group aims to invest in and expand AI infrastructure. Its first deal was a US$40 billion acquisition of Aligned Data Centres announced in October. Nvidia Corp, the Kuwait Investment Authority and Temasek Holdings Pte are also investors in AIP.

See also: EV sales are booming in Europe with gasoline at US$10 a gallon

Representatives for BlackRock, GIP, IFM, MGX, Blue Owl and Stack didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Stack’s Apac data centres are in Tokyo, Osaka, Melbourne, Sydney and Johor Bahru in Malaysia, its website shows.

title: US 30-year yield hits highest since 2004 as bond sell-off deepens
article:
(Sept 24): Yields on the US government’s longest-dated bonds climbed to the highest level in more than two decades, the latest milestone notched in an extended bond sell-off driven by inflation and fiscal concerns.

The rate on 30-year Treasuries rose as much as four basis points on Thursday to 5.44%, the highest since 2004, after Brent crude oil prices jumped. It follows a surge this week that left yields across maturities around the highest levels since 2007.

“People are running out of superlatives for the yield on the 30-year bond,” said Ed Al-Hussainy, a portfolio manager at Columbia Threadneedle. “Investors are saying, ‘Look, if we’re going to lock up our money for 30 years, we need much higher compensation.’”

Pressure on long-dated bonds has mounted as economic growth, elevated energy prices as well as inflation and heavier government borrowing prompt investors to demand more compensation for locking up money for decades.

The continued rise of the 30-year yield undercuts the Treasury Department’s efforts to bring down long-term borrowing costs. As the selloff intensified, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in mid-August expanded the government’s bond buyback programme in an effort to ease pressure — though it’s had little sustained impact in the market.

See also: Japan 10-year yield climbs to 1996 high as global rout deepens

title: EV sales are booming in Europe with gasoline at US$10 a gallon
article:
(Sept 24): After years of broadly unsuccessful efforts to wean drivers off combustion engines, sales of electric vehicles are surging in Europe thanks to the jump in fuel prices stoked by geopolitical upheaval.

Registrations of fully-electric cars soared 52% across the region in August compared with a year earlier, according to data published Thursday by the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association. Germany, the biggest market, led the gains with a three-quarter jump while sales in France more than doubled.

“When fuel prices rise, the issue of running costs becomes super concrete for customers,” Xavier Chardon, head of Stellantis NV’s Citroën brand, said in an interview. “Getting an EV no longer is a technology choice, it becomes an economic one.”

A major reason for the leap in EV demand is the increasing cost of running traditional engines powered by fossil fuels, which has shot higher with the rising price of oil.

The US-Israeli war on Iran is disrupting tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, pushing the average price of a liter of gasoline in Germany to a record €2.31 a liter (equivalent to US$10 per gallon). Diesel is even more expensive in the birthplace of the modern car, as Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries crimp global supplies.

See also: BlackRock, IFM close in on US$25 bil stack data centre deal — Bloomberg

European buyers shifting to EVs means that through August, more than one in three vehicles sold had a plug, up from just over one in four.

The picture is similar across the region, where the jump in fuel prices is hitting cash-strapped households already straining to make ends meet. Prices are up by more than a quarter across key markets.

It’s also hurting transport-dependent firms. For Charles Rivière, a 54-year-old fisherman from Luc-sur-Mer on France’s north coast, the mounting cost of fueling his van and boat means he needs a lot more Parisians to buy his seafood to make the roundtrip to the capital worthwhile.

See also: SoftBank offers record yields on jumbo junk bonds in AI push — Bloomberg

“I used to make a profit with only 12 or 13 clients in Paris,” Rivière said while preparing oysters during an outdoor community event in the French capital’s 14th arrondissement.

“Now I no longer come if I don’t have orders from at least 20 clients and increasingly there are fewer of them,” he added. “When I don’t come, I have zero income.”

For an expanding share of drivers, switching to battery power is the answer. In Germany, charging a mid-range or luxury EV at home currently costs about 70% less than fueling a gasoline-powered car, according to analysis by comparison website Verivox.

Electric cars were already gaining momentum in Europe earlier this year as carmakers rolled out more affordable models like Renault SA’s Twingo E-Tech city car that starts at €19,490 (US$22,353 or $28,587) and Volkswagen AG’s €37,890 Skoda Elroq compact SUV.

Throughout this year, the sharp increase in EV demand helped offset deep declines for vehicles running on fuel only. Overall deliveries in August rose 5.3%, the lobby group said.

Governments are also providing financial support, especially for less affluent households. German drivers below a certain income threshold can get as much as €6,000 off the purchase price for an EV. In France, a program can reduce monthly car payments to below €100 for some models such as the Citroën ë-C3 city car.

Concern about insufficient battery range is also fading. Ford Motor Co.’s Capri long-range EV crossover can travel more than 600km on a single charge, on a par with Volvo Car AB’s mid-range EX60.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Yet for Europe’s storied manufacturers, the long-awaited EV boom comes with a sting in the tail. The industry has seen tens of billions evaporate when hiccups in demand and abrupt regulation changes in the US forced them to resize sales expectations.

Opel-maker Stellantis led the writedowns with an unprecedented charge of €25.4 billion for last year. The Jeep and Ram maker faced additional pain after the US reversal on EV policy under President Donald Trump.

Manufacturers reacted by deepening cost-cutting measures already in place. VW, the region’s biggest manufacturer, is pushing through plans to double global job cuts to 100,000. On Friday, it slashed its profit forecast for this year due to a sharp contraction in China.

Europe’s struggles are opening up more inroads for Chinese manufacturers offering solid technology at affordable prices. BYD Co’s budget city EV Dolphin Surf starts at €22,990 and it’s also offering customers in Italy discounts of as much as €11,600. Chinese bands made up a record share of nearly 12% of total new-car sales in Europe in August, according to figures from Dataforce published Wednesday.

The impact of record fuel prices on voters is also reshaping European political agendas.

With Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s ruling coalition hemorrhaging voter support, Germany’s federal and state governments last week agreed to a €2.5 billion relief package for motorists and businesses. In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government this month introduced a vehicle ownership tax cut, ahead of a national election next year.

In France, concerns are mounting that the latest French cost-of-living crisis may trigger fresh unrest similar to the “yellow vest” protests in 2018. During the past week, fishermen blockaded several ports and a fuel depot along the Mediterranean coast and some gas stations in the northern part of the country were vandalised.

“Drivers are no longer filling up their tank completely,” according to Jacques Vaysse, owner of an independent gas station in Salles-Curan, a village in the Aveyron region in southeastern France. “There will be a social fallout unless the government cuts fuel taxes.”

title: Indonesia commodity export agency Danantara hires palm unit head
article:
(Sept 24): Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia is preparing to hire veteran vegetable-oil broker Daniel Lim to lead its palm oil division, according to people familiar with the matter, as the state-owned commodity agency builds out its senior team to oversee trade in one of the nation’s biggest exports.

DSI was set up earlier this year as an arm of the nation’s sovereign wealth fund, Danantara, after President Prabowo Subianto shocked markets by announcing he planned to centralize trade in raw materials. It aims to oversee exports of key commodities including palm oil and coal, scrutinizing transactions to avoid under-invoicing and transfer pricing — practices that Jakarta says can cost the state billions.

Singapore-based Lim was a managing director at agricultural commodities brokerage Tropical Oil ACI from 2014, according to his LinkedIn profile. Most recently, he worked as a trader at Golden Agri-Resources. Lim will join DSI once details have been finalized, the people said, asking not to be identified because the appointment hasn’t been made public.

Representatives from DSI did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Lim declined to comment.

DSI unveiled most of its senior leadership team in August, naming former Perusahaan Listrik Negara chief financial officer Sinthya Roesly as finance director, as well as PT Freeport Indonesia chief executive officer Tony Wenas and National Economic Council deputy chair Mari Elka Pangestu as commissioners. The agency is led by Luke Mahony, a former executive at nickel miner PT Vale Indonesia.

title: China plans inclusion of new products to expand derivatives trading link with Hong Kong
article:
(Sept 24): China plans to expand a major derivatives trading link with Hong Kong by granting global investors access to two onshore interest-rate products with standardised contracts, according to people familiar with the matter.

The China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) and the Shanghai Clearing House are working with OTC Clearing Hong Kong Ltd on adding standard interest rate swaps and standard bond forwards to the Swap Connect programme by 2028, said the people who requested anonymity discussing private information. The discussions are under the guidance of China’s central bank, they added.

The plan marks the latest move by authorities to further open up the world’s second-largest debt market to foreign capital as they look to internationalise the yuan and cement Hong Kong’s status as the top offshore hub for the currency. The two standardised onshore interest rate derivatives products have surged in popularity in recent years, thanks to more efficient settlements and the more targeted hedging they offer.

The People's Bank of China and CFETS didn’t immediately reply to separate requests for a comments. Shanghai Clearing House declined to comment.

“HKEX remains committed to working closely with regulators and market infrastructure partners to continuously enhance Swap Connect, support its sustainable long-term development and further strengthen Hong Kong’s role in advancing RMB internationalisation,” Hong Kong Exchange, the parent of the city’s clearing firm, said in a written response to Bloomberg’s queries.

Introduced in 2023, Swap Connect has been a key channel for global investors to protect their fixed income exposure in China’s local market against fluctuations in interest rates. The clearing volume under the trading link with Hong Kong rose to 1.7 trillion yuan (US$253 billion or $324 billion) in the second quarter, up nearly 48% on year, according to data from the Shanghai Clearing House.

See also: How Ford and GM can avoid VW’s China pains

Investors and businesses use interest rate swaps, or IRS, to hedge their interest rate exposure by exchanging a fixed-rate income stream for floating rates.

Compared with conventional IRS, which are over-the-counter (OTC) transactions with customised contracts between the counter-parties, standardised IRS carry uniform elements such as the pricing benchmark, maturity date, and tenor. They currently use the issuance rate of banks’ negotiable certificates of deposit as the reference rate in China’s onshore market.

The standardised bond forwards are linked to highly liquid policy bank notes issued by China Development Bank and Agricultural Development Bank of China.

See also: Taiwan plans to loosen offshore private fund investor limits

The two onshore standardised derivatives instruments adopt a centralised but anonymous price-bidding mechanism, which tends to attract better liquidity. They also feature central clearing, rather than more cumbersome bilateral settlement agreements.

Currently, the Swap Connect programme supports bilateral price quotations where the counterparties are identifiable before the transaction, with mandatory credit risk management agreements between them as a pre-requisite.

While traditional OTC-settled IRS continue to dominate China’s onshore market, the two standardised interest rate derivatives tools have become increasingly popular in recent years. The former’s clearing volume rose 36% on year to 44 trillion yuan in 2025, with the latter up 2.3 times to 13.8 trillion yuan, according to data from the Shanghai Clearing House.

title: Burnham signals reluctance to raise taxes in UK budget
article:
(Sept 24): UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham hinted he doesn’t want his government to repeat the tax rises of recent Labour budgets, as Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey prepares for a tricky financial statement on Oct 28.

Former Chancellor of the Exchequer Rachel Reeves delivered two budgets, raising taxes by a cumulative £68 billion (US$90 billion or $115 billion) in 2029-2030, according to Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) projections. That will lift the tax take to a record 38% of economic output at the end of the decade.

“We have had two budgets in 2024 and 2025 and we have to be conscious of the extent to which we have raised revenue,” Burnham told reporters travelling with him to the United Nations (UN) in New York this week. “We have to make sure we get the balance right.”

The Treasury has also previously indicated Healey, Reeves’ successor, does not want to implement a budget of the same scale. But most economists expect he will have to raise some taxes to help plug the gap in the public finances that has opened up as rising borrowing costs fueled by the US war in Iran erode the financial headroom he inherited.

Bloomberg Economics earlier this month estimated the surge in gilt yields would knock about £12 billion off the government’s £23.6 billion buffer. In an interview with the New Statesman published on Wednesday, Burnham said the UK has left itself “overexposed” to global bond markets, and defended controversial comments he made last year to the same publication that the UK should not be “in hock” to the global market.

See also: Burnham stands by remarks that UK is in hock to bond markets

As Healey prepares his budget, Treasury officials have looked at the possibility of hiking taxes on banks, oil and gas companies and gambling.

Burnham’s comments to reporters on the UN trip this week send a note of caution to those on the left of his party who believe he should raise more revenue so the government can spend more. Burnham declined to be drawn on whether the balance was right between taxing wealth and income, deferring that to the budget.

The premier acknowledged he faced a more difficult economic picture due to global conflicts, forcing a tonal shift ahead of the budget. But he said it was not true to suggest he had not been prepared for this.

See also: HMRC assigns tax compliance manager to every UK billionaire

“It’s not the case that we were surprised when we came in — not least because I was in access talks and understood very clearly the position,” Burnham said, referring to discussions his team had with ministries before he took over from Keir Starmer in July. “Because of the situation in the Middle East, the position changed, and has changed over the time I’ve been in. That’s just the reality.”

Bloomberg reported days before Burnham entered Downing Street that he was receiving gloomy internal economic assessments of rising inflation and a worsening economy thanks to the Iran war. Then in August Bloomberg obtained Treasury forecasts warning of a growth downgrade in 2027 if the conflict continued.

Despite the economic pressures, Burnham plans to use his first leader’s speech at Labour’s annual conference next week to project a message of hope and optimism.

“The message will be it’s time for Britain to believe again, it’s time for Britain to have hope again,” Burnham said. “A more stable Britain will be one that can then set out a new direction, drawing a line with the last decade.”

title: Europe needs more long-term LNG to avoid energy shocks, MET says
article:
(Sept 24): Europe needs more long-term contracts for seaborne gas supply to hedge against soaring prices, said the head of Swiss energy company MET Group.

European gas prices have more than doubled this year as the war in the Middle East has effectively cut off about a fifth of the world’s liquefied natural gas flows. Asian buyers are increasingly snapping up flexible spot cargoes — setting the stage for even fiercer competition between the regions this winter.

“A lot of long-term LNG supply globally goes to Asia, while Europe is still more spot-driven, and you can question how smart that is,” chief executive officer Huibert Vigeveno said in an interview. “Having more long-term contracts in Europe would certainly have helped this year.”

After losing most pipeline flows from Russia in 2022, Europe has increased its reliance on global LNG shipments, but utilities have been hesitant to commit to long-term contracts. Companies have focused on shorter and more flexible deals amid a projected decline in demand and stricter climate targets.

Europe has also slowed deals with the US, the world’s top LNG exporter, after relations between Washington and its European allies soured. While Brussels has warned against over-reliance on American fuel, Asian LNG buyers are accelerating discussions to buy more LNG from the US as the war in Iran drags on.

See also: Oil extends advance on renewed tensions between the US and Iran

The European Union stands out among top global importers for its reliance on the spot LNG market, according to the EU Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators. About 30% of the bloc’s LNG imports were spot-based in 2024 and the share remained high last year, according to the group known as ACER.

Prices have eased from this year’s peak earlier this month as traders closely follow renewed diplomatic efforts to stabilise energy flows from the Middle East. But uncertainty over supplies through the vital Strait of Hormuz remains.

“Even if Hormuz reopens, it will take at least three months for exports to ramp-up,” Vigeveno said, adding that prices risk rising again.

See also: Oil extends slump on Iran talks optimism, Saudi pipeline restart

“Earlier this year, we had expected European gas around €50 a megawatt-hour in winter if the Strait of Hormuz were to reopen in May, at €70 if that was July,” he said. “Now we could probably go up to €100 if Hormuz doesn’t reopen by the end of the winter, and that’s just supply-demand fundamentals.”

Meanwhile, MET is expanding and looking at potential transactions in northwest Europe, Vigeveno said, without providing more details.

“We have strong positions in central, eastern and southern Europe, but we would be interested to increase participation either organically or inorganically in Germany and other countries in Northwest Europe, in gas, LNG, power, and renewables,” he said.

The US, where MET buys substantial volumes of LNG, is also a focus, and the company is considering opening an office there, he added.

title: How Gen Z Investors in Singapore Can Start Investing
article:
Starting to invest can feel deceptively simple. Open an app, transfer money, and buy whatever stock, fund, or cryptocurrency is trending online.
The harder part is building an approach that can survive market declines, changing financial priorities, and years of regular contributions.
For Gen Z investors in Singapore, the advantage is time. Someone investing in their twenties may have several decades for returns to compound. But starting early only helps when the money is invested appropriately, costs remain under control, and short-term needs do not force the investor to sell during a market downturn.
Here is a practical sequence for getting started.
Build the Financial Foundation Before Buying Investments
The first step is not choosing a stock or opening a brokerage account. It is determining whether the money is ready to be invested.
Singapore’s
MoneySense Basic Financial Planning Guide
recommends setting aside at least three to six months of expenses as emergency savings. Someone with irregular freelance, gig, or commission-based income may need a larger buffer.
Emergency savings should remain accessible. Investing this money in shares creates the risk that it will fall in value just when it is needed for a medical bill, job loss, family emergency, or other unexpected expense.
High-interest debt should also be assessed first. Paying off a balance that charges a high and certain interest rate may be more beneficial than pursuing an uncertain investment return.
Only money that is not required for near-term spending should move into longer-term investments.
Define the Goal Before Choosing the Investment
“Building wealth” is too broad to determine what someone should invest in. A better starting point is to connect each amount of money to a goal and timeline.
A Gen Z investor could be saving for:
Further education within three years
A home deposit within five to eight years
Financial independence over several decades
Retirement through CPF, SRS, and personal investments
A flexible long-term fund with no fixed withdrawal date
The appropriate level of risk changes with the timeline. Money needed within a few years generally has less capacity to recover from a market decline. Longer-term money may be able to accept more short-term volatility in exchange for higher potential returns.
MoneySense notes that risk tolerance should reflect how much an investor can afford to lose, not simply how much the investor wants to earn. Its
guide to managing investment risk
recommends considering financial commitments, investment horizon, and capacity for loss when selecting an asset mix.
Decide How Much to Invest Each Month
There is no universal amount required to begin investing. What matters more is whether the contribution can be sustained without disrupting essential spending or emergency savings.
For example, someone earning S$3,000 a month might begin by investing S$200 or S$300 regularly rather than waiting to accumulate a large lump sum. This is only an illustration. The appropriate amount depends on expenses, debt, dependents, insurance needs, and financial goals.
Regular investing can also reduce the temptation to predict short-term market movements. Dollar-cost averaging involves investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, regardless of whether prices are rising or falling. This approach results in buying more units when prices are lower and fewer when they are higher.
Dollar-cost averaging does not prevent losses or guarantee better returns. Its main value is behavioural: it creates a consistent process and reduces dependence on market timing.
Choose Between Lower-Risk Assets and Growth Investments
A beginner does not need to start with individual stocks. The first investment should match the goal rather than what is receiving the most attention online.
Singapore Savings Bonds and T-bills
Money that may be needed sooner could be allocated to lower-risk instruments.
Singapore Savings Bonds are backed by the Singapore Government and can be redeemed monthly without a capital loss, although investors do not receive accrued interest for the month of redemption. The minimum investment is S$500, and an individual can hold up to S$200,000, according to the
Monetary Authority of Singapore
.
Treasury bills, or T-bills, are short-term Singapore Government Securities. The minimum application is S$1,000 in multiples of S$1,000, according to
MAS guidance for individual investors
. Unlike Savings Bonds, T-bills are designed to be held until maturity. Investors who sell before maturity may receive more or less than their original investment depending on market conditions.
These instruments offer lower potential returns than shares but may be more appropriate for capital that cannot tolerate large fluctuations.
Broad-Market Exchange-Traded Funds
For long-term growth, a diversified exchange-traded fund can provide exposure to many securities through a single investment.
An ETF is a fund listed and traded on an exchange. Many ETFs aim to track an index rather than select individual companies. An index-tracking ETF allows investors to gain exposure to an index without purchasing every component separately. Its management fees also tend to be lower than those of actively managed funds.
However, “ETF” does not automatically mean safe or diversified. Some funds concentrate on one country, industry, commodity, or investment theme. Others use derivatives, leverage, or synthetic structures. Investors should check:
What index or assets the ETF tracks
Which countries and industries dominate the portfolio
Whether the fund holds the underlying assets directly
Its expense ratio and other charges
Trading liquidity and bid-ask spread
The currency of the fund and its underlying investments
Whether it distributes or reinvests income
Whether it is classified as a Specified Investment Product
ETFs are not principal-guaranteed. Their prices can decline, and investors may lose a substantial part of their investment.
Individual Stocks
Buying individual shares gives an investor direct exposure to particular companies, but it also introduces company-specific risk.
Before purchasing a stock, investors should understand how the business makes money, whether it is profitable, how much debt it carries, the quality of management, its valuation, and the risks facing its industry.
Review company annual reports, corporate announcements, financial performance, governance, and vulnerabilities before investing. SGX-listed shares are generally traded in board lots of 100, although the amount required depends on the share price and applicable lot size.
A beginner who wants to research individual companies could use them as a smaller part of a broader portfolio rather than placing the entire investment in one or two familiar brands.
Open an Account Without Choosing a Platform Based on Promotions
Investors need a trading or investment account before they can purchase shares, ETFs, or managed portfolios. The decision should not be based solely on sign-up rewards, free shares, or temporary commission offers.
Before opening an account, compare:
Brokerage commission and minimum fees
Platform and custody charges
Foreign-exchange conversion costs
Market access
Recurring investment features
Minimum investment amounts
How securities are held
Fees for transferring securities to another provider
Access to shareholder voting and corporate actions
What happens to client assets if the platform stops operating
For SGX-listed securities, holdings may be kept in an investor’s CDP Securities Account or through a broker’s custody account. SGX confirms that securities purchased in the Singapore market can be held through either structure in its
CDP guidance
.
With a direct CDP account, eligible Singapore-listed securities are recorded in the investor’s account with the Central Depository. Under a broker-custody arrangement, the broker or its depository agent holds the securities for clients. Costs, access to corporate actions, shareholder rights, and transfer procedures can differ, so investors should understand the arrangement before funding the account.
Investors should also verify the provider through the
MAS Financial Institutions Directory
and check the
MAS Investor Alert List
. The Alert List identifies entities that may have been wrongly perceived as licensed or regulated by MAS, but it should not be treated as a complete list of every potentially problematic entity.
Watch the Percentage Cost of Small Investments
Low advertised commissions do not always mean low total costs.
An investor making a S$100 purchase and paying S$2 in total transaction costs loses 2% before the investment generates any return. The same S$2 cost on a S$1,000 purchase is 0.2%.
Other costs can include:
Currency-conversion spreads
Custody or platform fees
Fund expense ratios
Bid-ask spreads
Withdrawal or transfer fees
Taxes withheld on foreign dividends
Sales charges for managed products
This does not mean beginners must wait until they have thousands of dollars. It means the purchase size and frequency should make sense relative to the fees. A recurring plan with low percentage costs may be more efficient than making many small manual trades.
Treat CPF and SRS as Separate Decisions
Cash, CPF savings, and SRS funds serve different purposes and should not automatically be invested in the same way.
CPF Investment Scheme
The CPF Investment Scheme allows eligible members to invest part of their Ordinary Account or Special Account savings in approved products. For CPFIS-OA, members must first set aside S$20,000 in their Ordinary Account. Investments in stocks are also limited to 35% of investible savings, according to the
CPF Board
.
Using CPF money carries an opportunity cost because CPF savings already earn interest. An investment must outperform the applicable CPF interest rate after fees to leave the member better off. Investors should therefore avoid using CPF simply because the option is available.
Supplementary Retirement Scheme
The Supplementary Retirement Scheme is voluntary and is designed to complement CPF savings. Contributions may qualify for tax relief, while investment returns accumulate tax-free before withdrawal. Only 50% of qualifying withdrawals at retirement are taxable.
The annual contribution limit is S$15,300 for Singapore citizens and permanent residents and S$35,700 for foreigners, according to
IRAS
.
SRS is most relevant to investors who pay income tax and can leave the money invested for retirement. Early withdrawals are generally subject to tax and a 5% penalty, so it is not an appropriate substitute for emergency savings.
Understand the Singapore Tax Position, but Check Foreign Taxes Too
Dividends paid by Singapore-resident companies
under the one-tier corporate tax system are generally not taxable for individual shareholders.
Gains from selling shares and other financial instruments are also generally treated as non-taxable personal investment gains. However, IRAS may treat gains as taxable when the activity constitutes trading rather than personal investing. Its
guidance on gains from financial instruments
explains the distinction.
Foreign investments may be subject to taxes in the market where the asset is based, including withholding tax on dividends. Investors should check the treatment of the specific market, security, and account instead of assuming that Singapore’s tax rules are the only ones that apply.
Avoid Turning Investing Into Online Entertainment
Gen Z investors have immediate access to market news, trading communities, influencers, and real-time price movements. Access to information can be useful, but it can also encourage unnecessary trading and excessive risk-taking.
Warning signs include:
Buying mainly because an asset is trending online
Copying trades without understanding the investment
Treating screenshots of profits as evidence of repeatable skill
Borrowing money or using margin to invest
Concentrating most of a portfolio in one company, industry, or cryptocurrency
Assuming a high dividend yield means an investment is safe
Confusing a rising price with improving business fundamentals
Trading frequently without calculating total costs
Leverage deserves particular caution. Margin financing can produce losses beyond the amount initially invested, depending on the position taken.
A regulated platform also does not make every product offered through it appropriate for every investor. Product risk and platform legitimacy are separate questions.
A Practical First-Month Investing Checklist
A new investor can use the following sequence:
Calculate average monthly essential expenses.
Build or confirm an emergency fund covering at least three to six months.
Review high-interest debt and near-term financial commitments.
Define the goal, target amount, and expected investment period.
Decide how much can be invested consistently each month.
Compare lower-risk assets, diversified funds, and individual shares.
Verify any provider through the MAS Financial Institutions Directory.
Compare total fees rather than headline commissions.
Start with an amount small enough to tolerate market fluctuations.
Automate contributions where practical and review the portfolio periodically.
The review should focus on whether the portfolio still matches the goal, risk tolerance, and timeline. Checking prices several times a day is not the same as monitoring an investment.
Starting Small Without Losing Sight of the Long Term
A Gen Z investor in Singapore does not need a large salary, a portfolio of popular stocks, or the ability to predict the next market rally to begin investing.
The more important starting points are a sufficient emergency fund, a defined goal, a realistic monthly contribution, an appropriately diversified portfolio, and a clear understanding of costs and risks.
Starting early creates more time for compounding, but time cannot compensate for excessive fees, weak diversification, leverage, or investments that do not match the investor’s needs. The objective is not simply to enter the market as soon as possible. It is to build a process that can be sustained through changing markets and life stages.

title: Can AI Simplify Investing? What Singapore Beginners Should Actually Expect
article:
Type a stock ticker into an AI chatbot with access to current market data, and within seconds, you may get a summary of recent earnings, an overview of market sentiment, and a plain-English explanation of what it could mean. Research that once required investors to search through multiple filings, reports, and data platforms can now be condensed quickly on a phone. That helps explain why AI tools are becoming a more familiar part of retail investing. An
Investing.com survey of 938 U.S. investors
conducted in March 2026 found that 62% had used AI to help inform an investment decision, with 23.6% saying they used it regularly.
For beginners in Singapore, the pitch is tempting: let the algorithm handle the heavy lifting and start investing with more confidence sooner. But does AI actually simplify investing or does it just make the noise louder? Here is what these tools genuinely do well, where they are already showing up locally, and where beginners still need to bring their own judgment.
What Do AI and Automated Investing Tools Actually Do?
The tools commonly grouped under “AI investing” generally fall into two broad categories, and it helps to understand the difference before relying on either one.
Robo-advisors
are the more established form of automated investing. You answer questions about your goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance, and the platform builds and manages a diversified portfolio for you. Many use established asset-allocation models, including approaches based on Modern Portfolio Theory, to balance expected risk and return. From there, the robo-advisor may handle rebalancing, automatically buying and selling investments to keep the portfolio close to its target allocation as markets move.
AI research and screening tools
are newer and more varied. They include chatbots that summarize financial filings, tools that screen stocks using technical or fundamental data, and sentiment trackers that assess whether coverage of a company is turning bullish or bearish. The
Investing.com survey
found that investors primarily used AI to research stocks and other assets, understand market news, generate trading ideas, and help make portfolio decisions.
Put together, the honest case for AI investing tools is efficiency, not prediction. They can process more information faster than a person scrolling through filings on a lunch break. What they cannot reliably do is tell you which stock is about to take off.
How Are Singapore Investors Already Using Automation?
Singapore has one of the more developed robo-advisory markets in the region,
with more than 10 platforms
offering automated investment services. Before investing, users should confirm that a provider holds the relevant Monetary Authority of Singapore licence and understand how their assets will be held. Leading licensed robo-advisors generally place client assets in segregated trust or custodian accounts, separate from the provider’s own assets. Investors can verify a provider’s regulatory status through the
MAS Financial Institutions Directory
.
Within that market, the approaches vary. Endowus allows eligible investors to invest CPF and SRS savings through managed portfolios, charging an
annual access fee of approximately 0.40%
for CPF and SRS portfolios. StashAway uses what it calls an
Economic Regime-based Asset Allocation framework
, which adjusts portfolio allocations based on broader economic conditions. Syfe offers ETF-based portfolios alongside
cash-management products
. Some providers combine technology with human oversight rather than relying entirely on automated decisions. Phillip SMART Portfolio, for example, describes its approach as a “
Cyborg Methodology
”, combining artificial intelligence with input from professional portfolio managers.
The common thread is that automation does not eliminate the need for a regulated financial provider, custodian, or underlying investment account. Instead, these platforms use technology to simplify activities such as risk assessment, portfolio construction, investing, monitoring, and rebalancing.
Where Does AI Fall Short, and What Is MAS Watching?
AI’s blind spots matter as much as its strengths. In the Investing.com survey,
53.5% of respondents
said they trusted AI-generated investment analysis to some extent but still verified the information elsewhere. That instinct is reasonable. The survey also found that 24.2% were concerned about market herding, which can occur when many investors react to the same AI-generated signals or information at the same time.
MAS is also paying closer attention to how financial institutions use AI. In November 2025, the regulator published a
consultation paper on proposed AI risk-management guidelines
. The proposed guidelines address areas such as senior-management oversight, risk assessment, model development and testing, monitoring, and the use of third-party AI. For everyday investors, this does not mean every AI tool is unsafe or directly regulated by MAS. It means users should distinguish between AI features offered by licensed financial institutions and general-purpose chatbots that may not be designed or regulated to provide investment advice.
AI and automated investing tools genuinely simplify parts of investing. They speed up research, automate tasks such as rebalancing, and make sophisticated analytical capabilities accessible on a beginner’s budget. What they do not replace is the judgment every investor eventually has to exercise: how much risk to take, which information to trust, and when to walk away from an investment. For a first-time investor in Singapore, AI may be most useful as a fast, tireless research assistant, while a licensed platform can automate parts of portfolio management within a regulated environment. Neither is a substitute for understanding what you are putting your money into.
